FALSE CHILD ABUSE ALLEGATION SANCTIONS AND REPORTING PROTECTIONS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Jordan Lee

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet explains three related provisions of the California Family Code that can come into play when an allegation of child abuse is made during a custody or visitation proceeding between Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee regarding Alex Morgan-Lee, case number 26FL00123, filed in Sacramento County: the court's authority under Family Code section 3027 to take temporary protective steps and request an agency investigation, the monetary-sanctions remedy under Family Code section 3027.1 for an accusation later found false and knowingly so, and the reporting protections and false-report limitation under Family Code section 3027.5. It states the text of these statutes and how published California Court of Appeal decisions have described and applied them. It does not state whether any allegation made in this proceeding is true or false, whether a motion for sanctions should be filed or opposed, or what the court is likely to do, and it is not a substitute for advice from a licensed attorney about the facts of a specific matter.

TEMPORARY PROTECTIVE STEPS WHILE AN ALLEGATION IS PENDING
Family Code section 3027(a) states that if allegations of child abuse, including child sexual abuse, are made during a child custody proceeding and the court has concerns regarding the child's safety, the court may take any reasonable, temporary steps it deems appropriate under the circumstances, in its discretion, to protect the child's safety until an investigation can be completed. The statute states that nothing in the section affects the separate applicability of Welfare and Institutions Code sections 16504 or 16506, which concern child welfare services investigations and case plans.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "If allegations of child abuse, including child sexual abuse, are made during a child custody proceeding and the court has concerns regarding the child’s safety, the court may take any reasonable, temporary steps as the court, in its discretion, deems appropriate under the circumstances to protect the child’s safety until an investigation can be completed. Nothing in this section shall affect the applicability of Section 16504 or 16506 of the Welfare and Institutions Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3027(a) (California Legislative Information text), a court's authority to take reasonable temporary protective steps when child abuse allegations, including child sexual abuse, arise during a custody proceeding and the court has safety concerns (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3027.)
  Known gap: The statute does not enumerate what 'reasonable, temporary steps' a court may take, and leaves that choice to the court's discretion under the circumstances of each case; this clause does not predict what steps a court would take in any particular case. It also does not cover subdivision (b) of section 3027, the agency-investigation-referral provision, which is addressed in a separate clause. The statute is triggered by allegations being made and the court having 'concerns regarding the child's safety' — it does not require that the allegation be shown true, or even plausible, before temporary steps may be taken, and it does not state what showing is needed to establish such 'concerns.'

THE COURT'S DISCRETION TO REQUEST A CHILD WELFARE AGENCY INVESTIGATION
Family Code section 3027(b) states that if allegations of child abuse, including child sexual abuse, are made during a child custody proceeding, the court may request that the local child welfare services agency conduct an investigation of the allegations under Welfare and Institutions Code section 328, and that upon completing the investigation the agency must report its findings to the court.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "If allegations of child abuse, including child sexual abuse, are made during a child custody proceeding, the court may request that the local child welfare services agency conduct an investigation of the allegations pursuant to Section 328 of the Welfare and Institutions Code. Upon completion of the investigation, the agency shall report its findings to the court."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3027(b) (California Legislative Information text), a court's discretion to request a local child welfare services agency investigation of child abuse allegations made during a custody proceeding, and the agency's duty to report findings (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3027.)
  Known gap: The statute uses 'may request,' not 'must' or 'shall request' — a family court is not required to request an agency investigation merely because an allegation has been made, and this clause does not describe what factors, if any, guide that discretionary choice. It also does not examine Welfare and Institutions Code section 328 itself, which governs the mechanics, timing, or scope of the agency's own investigation once requested. The source statute's official published text line-wraps mid-phrase between 'conduct an investigation of the' and 'allegations pursuant to Section 328' (verified directly against the raw fetched leginfo.legislature.ca.gov HTML, where a literal line break and indentation whitespace appear at that point with no missing or added words); the quote below renders that wrap as a normal single space, consistent with ordinary sentence flow.

SANCTIONS FOR A KNOWINGLY FALSE ACCUSATION: THE STATUTORY ELEMENTS
Family Code section 3027.1(a) states that if a court determines, based on the section 3027 investigation or other evidence presented to it, that an accusation of child abuse or neglect made during a child custody proceeding is false and the person making the accusation knew it to be false when it was made, the court may impose reasonable money sanctions against that person, not to exceed all costs the accused party incurred as a direct result of defending the accusation, plus reasonable attorney's fees incurred in recovering the sanctions. The statute defines 'person' for this purpose to include a witness, a party, or a party's attorney, so the sanctions remedy can reach someone other than the party who was accusing the other party.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "If a court determines, based on the investigation described in Section 3027 or other evidence presented to it, that an accusation of child abuse or neglect made during a child custody proceeding is false and the person making the accusation knew it to be false at the time the accusation was made, the court may impose reasonable money sanctions, not to exceed all costs incurred by the party accused as a direct result of defending the accusation, and reasonable attorney’s fees incurred in recovering the sanctions, against the person making the accusation. For the purposes of this section, “person” includes a witness, a party, or a party’s attorney."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3027.1(a) (California Legislative Information text), the elements for a discretionary monetary-sanctions award against a person who made a knowingly false child abuse or neglect accusation during a custody proceeding, its cap, and its definition of 'person' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3027.1.)
  Known gap: The statute makes a sanctions award discretionary ('may impose'), not automatic, even where a court has found an accusation false and knowingly so — this clause does not describe how courts exercise that discretion. It does not define 'reasonable money sanctions' numerically, and it caps the award at costs actually incurred defending the specific accusation, not general litigation costs in the broader custody case. It also does not cover the false-accusation timing deadline or the order-to-show-cause procedure required to seek these sanctions, each addressed in separate clauses.

THE ORDER-TO-SHOW-CAUSE PROCEDURE, 15-DAY NOTICE, AND CUMULATIVE REMEDY
Family Code section 3027.1(b) states that on motion by any person requesting sanctions under the section, the court must issue an order to show cause why the requested sanctions should not be imposed; that order must be served on the person against whom sanctions are sought, and a hearing on it must be scheduled at least 15 days after the order is served. Section 3027.1(c) states that the remedy the section provides is in addition to any other remedy provided by law, meaning it does not by its terms replace other statutory or common-law remedies that might otherwise be available.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "On motion by any person requesting sanctions under this section, the court shall issue its order to show cause why the requested sanctions should not be imposed. The order to show cause shall be served on the person against whom the sanctions are sought and a hearing thereon shall be scheduled by the court to be conducted at least 15 days after the order is served."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3027.1(b) (California Legislative Information text), the order-to-show-cause procedure and 15-day minimum notice period before a hearing on a section 3027.1 sanctions motion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3027.1.)
  "The remedy provided by this section is in addition to any other remedy provided by law."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3027.1(c) (California Legislative Information text), the section 3027.1 remedy is cumulative, in addition to any other remedy provided by law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3027.1.)
  Known gap: This clause covers only the procedural mechanics stated in subdivisions (b) and (c); it does not state a deadline for when, relative to the underlying custody proceeding or the judgment resolving the abuse allegation, a section 3027.1 motion must first be filed — the statute itself is silent on that question, which published case law has since addressed and is described in a separate clause. It also does not describe what other remedies subdivision (c)'s 'in addition to any other remedy' language might reach in a given case, or how courts reconcile overlapping sanctions requests under section 3027.1 and other statutes such as section 271. The source statute's official published text line-wraps mid-phrase within subdivision (b), between 'a hearing thereon shall be' and 'scheduled by the court' (verified directly against the raw fetched leginfo.legislature.ca.gov HTML, where a literal line break and indentation whitespace appear at that point with no missing or added words); the quote below renders that wrap as a normal single space.

CASE LAW: A PRESUMPTIVE FILING DEADLINE, AND STRICT ENFORCEMENT OF THE NOTICE PROCEDURE
Because section 3027.1 does not itself state a deadline for filing a sanctions motion, one published Court of Appeal decision addressed the question as one of first impression. The court held that, absent further direction from the Legislature, equitable principles govern the timing of a section 3027.1 motion, and that a party moving for section 3027.1 sanctions should file the motion on or before the earliest of two dates measured from the judgment or order exonerating that party of the child abuse or neglect allegations: 60 days after that judgment or order is served, or 180 days after it is entered. The court described these deadlines as drawn by analogy from California Rules of Court provisions governing motions for attorney's fees in civil proceedings, which also apply in family law cases; a party who files after these presumptive deadlines bears the burden of showing the delay was excusable and did not unduly prejudice the person the motion is directed against. A second published decision illustrates that the statute's own procedural requirements are enforced strictly: where a party sought section 3027.1 sanctions over an opponent's alleged false abuse allegations but did so within a written closing argument, rather than by the order-to-show-cause procedure with the required 15-day advance notice of a hearing, the Court of Appeal held the trial court correctly declined to award sanctions on that defective request.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "Section 3027.1 gives a court discretion to impose monetary sanctions against a party, the party’s attorney or a witness if the moving party establishes that the accusation of child abuse or neglect was made in a child custody proceeding, the accusation was false and the person or persons making it knew it was false when the accusation was made."
  — Robert J. v. Catherine D. (2009) 171 Cal.App.4th 1500, elements of a section 3027.1 sanctions claim, restated by the Court of Appeal (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2256763/robert-j-v-catherine-d/)
  "60 days after the judgment or order exonerating him or her from child abuse or neglect allegations is served, or 180 days from the entry of such judgment or order."
  — Robert J. v. Catherine D. (2009) 171 Cal.App.4th 1500, the presumptive deadline the Court of Appeal established for filing a section 3027.1 sanctions motion (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2256763/robert-j-v-catherine-d/)
  "Niko asserts the trial court erred in not awarding sanctions pursuant to sections 3027.1 and 271 based on Foreman’s false allegations of abuse."
  — Niko v. Foreman (2006) 144 Cal.App.4th 344, the party's own request for section 3027.1 sanctions over the opponent's alleged false abuse allegations (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2290411/niko-v-foreman/)
  "Niko was required to serve an OSC regarding section 3027.1 sanctions against Foreman at least 15 days before a scheduled hearing on the matter"
  — Niko v. Foreman (2006) 144 Cal.App.4th 344, strict enforcement of section 3027.1's order-to-show-cause and 15-day notice procedure, and the resulting denial of sanctions (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2290411/niko-v-foreman/)
  Known gap: The timing deadline described here comes from a single published Court of Appeal decision (Robert J. v. Catherine D.) applying equitable principles by analogy to civil-fee-motion timing rules; because it was announced as an issue of first impression, that same decision also held its own new procedural rule should not be applied retroactively to the party before it — this clause does not track whether or how later decisions have applied, narrowed, or extended this timing rule, and CourtListener's search index was not queried for every possible later citing case given this document's research budget. The second decision (Niko v. Foreman) denying sanctions for noncompliance with the order-to-show-cause and notice procedure does not establish that a properly noticed section 3027.1 motion filed in a written closing argument would always fail — the court's holding turned on the absence of both a hearing and the statutorily required notice opportunity, not on the closing-argument format standing alone. Neither decision was located through a search for case law interpreting section 3027.5 specifically, and no case law is cited in this document's clauses covering that section for that reason.

PROTECTION FOR A PARENT WHO LAWFULLY REPORTED OR INVESTIGATED SUSPECTED SEXUAL ABUSE
Family Code section 3027.5(a) states that a parent must not be placed on supervised visitation, denied custody of or visitation with the parent's child, or have custody or visitation rights limited, solely because that parent lawfully reported suspected sexual abuse of the child; otherwise acted lawfully, based on a reasonable belief, to determine whether the child was a victim of sexual abuse; or sought treatment for the child from a licensed mental health professional for suspected sexual abuse.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "A parent shall not be placed on supervised visitation, or be denied custody of or visitation with the parent’s child, and custody or visitation rights shall not be limited, solely because the parent did any of the following: (1) Lawfully reported suspected sexual abuse of the child. (2) Otherwise acted lawfully, based on a reasonable belief, to determine if the child was the victim of sexual abuse. (3) Sought treatment for the child from a licensed mental health professional for suspected sexual abuse."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3027.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), the bar on placing a parent on supervised visitation or limiting custody or visitation solely because the parent lawfully reported suspected sexual abuse, lawfully investigated it, or sought treatment for the child (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3027.5.)
  Known gap: This protection is limited by its own terms to child sexual abuse, not child abuse or neglect generally — sections 3027 and 3027.1, by contrast, apply to 'child abuse or neglect' without that limitation. The statute's protection also applies only where one of the listed acts was the sole reason for the custody or visitation limitation ('solely because'); it does not state how a court is to determine whether a limitation imposed for stated reasons that include, but are not limited to, a listed act falls inside or outside that protection. It does not itself define 'lawfully reported' or what counts as 'a reasonable belief' for the second listed act.

THE STATUTORY EXCEPTION: A KNOWINGLY FALSE SEXUAL ABUSE REPORT MADE TO INTERFERE WITH THE OTHER PARENT
Family Code section 3027.5(b) states the limits of the protection described in subdivision (a): a court may order supervised visitation or limit a parent's custody or visitation if it finds substantial evidence that the parent, intending to interfere with the other parent's lawful contact with the child, made a report of child sexual abuse — during the custody proceeding or at any other time — that the reporting parent knew was false when made. The statute further states that any such limitation, whether imposed under this subdivision or under a different statute addressing a false child abuse report, may be imposed only after the court has determined the limitation is necessary to protect the child's health, safety, and welfare, and only after the court has considered the state's policy, declared in Family Code section 3020(b), of ensuring children have frequent and continuing contact with both parents.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "The court may order supervised visitation or limit a parent’s custody or visitation if the court finds substantial evidence that the parent, with the intent to interfere with the other parent’s lawful contact with the child, made a report of child sexual abuse, during a child custody proceeding or at any other time, that the reporting parent knew was false at the time it was made."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3027.5(b) (California Legislative Information text), the substantial-evidence finding required before a court may limit custody or visitation for a knowingly false sexual abuse report made to interfere with the other parent's contact (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3027.5.)
  "A limitation of custody or visitation, including an order for supervised visitation, pursuant to this subdivision, or a statute regarding the making of a false child abuse report, shall be imposed only after the court has determined that the limitation is necessary to protect the health, safety, and welfare of the child, and the court has considered the state’s policy of ensuring that children have frequent and continuing contact with both parents as declared in subdivision (b) of Section 3020."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3027.5(b) (California Legislative Information text), the required best-interest finding and consideration of the frequent-and-continuing-contact policy before any such limitation, including under a different false-report statute (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3027.5.)
  Known gap: The statute requires 'substantial evidence' of both the parent's knowledge that the report was false and an intent to interfere with the other parent's lawful contact — it does not define that evidentiary standard for this specific context or state how it compares to the standards used elsewhere in the Family Code, including the 'knew it to be false' standard in section 3027.1. This clause does not describe Family Code section 3020(b)'s text directly (only that section 3027.5(b) cross-references it), and no case law construing section 3027.5(b) was located within this document's CourtListener research budget — the two published decisions cited elsewhere in this document (Robert J. v. Catherine D. and Niko v. Foreman) address section 3027.1, not section 3027.5, and neither was found by a targeted search for section 3027.5 case law.

HOW THESE STATUTES DIFFER FROM RELATED FAMILY LAW TOPICS
These statutes are distinct from several other family-law topics that can arise in the same custody proceeding. They are not the Family Code section 3044 rebuttable presumption against awarding custody to a parent who has perpetrated domestic violence, which turns on a judicial finding of domestic violence rather than on the truth or falsity of an abuse allegation. They are not the mandated-reporter laws under the Child Abuse and Neglect Reporting Act, which impose independent reporting duties on certain professionals regardless of any custody proceeding. They are not a domestic violence restraining order or a civil harassment restraining order, which are separate proceedings with their own statutory standards. And a section 3027.1 sanctions motion is not the same statute as a Family Code section 271 sanctions motion for litigation conduct that furthers or frustrates settlement, though the two are sometimes sought together, as illustrated by the case law discussed elsewhere in this document.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee acknowledge having reviewed this information sheet describing Family Code sections 3027, 3027.1, and 3027.5 as they may relate to the custody or visitation proceeding concerning Alex Morgan-Lee, case number 26FL00123, filed in Sacramento County, including the court's authority to take temporary protective steps and request an agency investigation, the elements, cap, and procedure for a section 3027.1 sanctions motion, the presumptive filing deadline and procedural requirements described in the case law discussed above, and the reporting protections and false-report limitation under section 3027.5. Signed in Oakland, California on September 7, 2026.

citations.cite: the bar on placing a parent on supervised visitation or limiting custody or visitation solely because the parent lawfully reported suspected sexual abuse, lawfully investigated it, or sought treatment for the child
citations.quote: A parent shall not be placed on supervised visitation, or be denied custody of or visitation with the parent’s child, and custody or visitation rights shall not be limited, solely because the parent did any of the following: (1) Lawfully reported suspected sexual abuse of the child. (2) Otherwise acted lawfully, based on a reasonable belief, to determine if the child was the victim of sexual abuse. (3) Sought treatment for the child from a licensed mental health professional for suspected sexual abuse.

expectedJSON.gap: This protection is limited by its own terms to child sexual abuse, not child abuse or neglect generally — sections 3027 and 3027.1, by contrast, apply to 'child abuse or neglect' without that limitation. The statute's protection also applies only where one of the listed acts was the sole reason for the custody or visitation limitation ('solely because'); it does not state how a court is to determine whether a limitation imposed for stated reasons that include, but are not limited to, a listed act falls inside or outside that protection. It does not itself define 'lawfully reported' or what counts as 'a reasonable belief' for the second listed act.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code section 3027.5(b) states the limits of the protection described in subdivision (a): a court may order supervised visitation or limit a parent's custody or visitation if it finds substantial evidence that the parent, intending to interfere with the other parent's lawful contact with the child, made a report of child sexual abuse — during the custody proceeding or at any other time — that the reporting parent knew was false when made. The statute further states that any such limitation, whether imposed under this subdivision or under a different statute addressing a false child abuse report, may be imposed only after the court has determined the limitation is necessary to protect the child's health, safety, and welfare, and only after the court has considered the state's policy, declared in Family Code section 3020(b), of ensuring children have frequent and continuing contact with both parents.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3027.5(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the substantial-evidence finding required before a court may limit custody or visitation for a knowingly false sexual abuse report made to interfere with the other parent's contact
citations.quote: The court may order supervised visitation or limit a parent’s custody or visitation if the court finds substantial evidence that the parent, with the intent to interfere with the other parent’s lawful contact with the child, made a report of child sexual abuse, during a child custody proceeding or at any other time, that the reporting parent knew was false at the time it was made.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3027.5(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the required best-interest finding and consideration of the frequent-and-continuing-contact policy before any such limitation, including under a different false-report statute
citations.quote: A limitation of custody or visitation, including an order for supervised visitation, pursuant to this subdivision, or a statute regarding the making of a false child abuse report, shall be imposed only after the court has determined that the limitation is necessary to protect the health, safety, and welfare of the child, and the court has considered the state’s policy of ensuring that children have frequent and continuing contact with both parents as declared in subdivision (b) of Section 3020.

expectedJSON.gap: The statute requires 'substantial evidence' of both the parent's knowledge that the report was false and an intent to interfere with the other parent's lawful contact — it does not define that evidentiary standard for this specific context or state how it compares to the standards used elsewhere in the Family Code, including the 'knew it to be false' standard in section 3027.1. This clause does not describe Family Code section 3020(b)'s text directly (only that section 3027.5(b) cross-references it), and no case law construing section 3027.5(b) was located within this document's CourtListener research budget — the two published decisions cited elsewhere in this document (Robert J. v. Catherine D. and Niko v. Foreman) address section 3027.1, not section 3027.5, and neither was found by a targeted search for section 3027.5 case law.

expectedJSON.body: These statutes are distinct from several other family-law topics that can arise in the same custody proceeding. They are not the Family Code section 3044 rebuttable presumption against awarding custody to a parent who has perpetrated domestic violence, which turns on a judicial finding of domestic violence rather than on the truth or falsity of an abuse allegation. They are not the mandated-reporter laws under the Child Abuse and Neglect Reporting Act, which impose independent reporting duties on certain professionals regardless of any custody proceeding. They are not a domestic violence restraining order or a civil harassment restraining order, which are separate proceedings with their own statutory standards. And a section 3027.1 sanctions motion is not the same statute as a Family Code section 271 sanctions motion for litigation conduct that furthers or frustrates settlement, though the two are sometimes sought together, as illustrated by the case law discussed elsewhere in this document.

Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee acknowledge having reviewed this information sheet describing Family Code sections 3027, 3027.1, and 3027.5 as they may relate to the custody or visitation proceeding concerning Alex Morgan-Lee, case number 26FL00123, filed in Sacramento County, including the court's authority to take temporary protective steps and request an agency investigation, the elements, cap, and procedure for a section 3027.1 sanctions motion, the presumptive filing deadline and procedural requirements described in the case law discussed above, and the reporting protections and false-report limitation under section 3027.5. Signed in Oakland, California on September 7, 2026.
